## **Target Demographics and Positioning**

Taco Bell's core audience has always been younger consumers - Gen Z and millennials, broadly ages 18 to 34. But the more interesting thing about their positioning is that they don't just sell to this group, they _talk like_ this group. 

Their social content leans into **meme culture, self-aware humor, and internet-native references**.

It’s safe to say that Taco Bell’s digital presence is actually bringing in sales and loyalty.

## **All About Live Más LIVE **

The genius of Live Más LIVE starts with one structural insight: instead of drip-feeding product announcements throughout the year, Taco Bell made one giant, singular moment of it. 

Traditionally, restaurant chains send out releases and other marketing materials as the year goes on, in advance of their introduction. 

Taco Bell flipped that entirely - they **concentrated all the year's innovation into a single event**, created scarcity and anticipation around it, and let that moment carry them through the rest of the year.

The very first event kicked off on February 9, 2024 in Las Vegas, NV. 

The livestreamed keynote introduced over 30 new products across **Taco Bell's development pipeline, test, and national launches**.

Youtube: Taco Bell Presents Live Más Live 2024 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VnufDp8dCnE)

The first event was patterned after Apple's annual Worldwide Developers Conference - only for Crunchwraps rather than iPhones. 

Apple's WWDC is built around the idea that people _wait for it_ - it's appointment media. 

It has **hype cycles, leaks, fan speculation, and hot takes**. 

Taco Bell looked at that model and decided there was _no reason a fast food brand couldn't create the same dynamic_.

Traditional Fast Food PR: 

**Press Release - Industry Trades - Disjointed Local Ads - Passive Consumer **

Taco Bell's Live Mas Playbook: 

**Live Keynote - Superfan Evangelism - Viral Social Hype - Active App Adoption**

Taco Bell FIRE! Tier Rewards Members had the first chance to score tickets, hotel accommodations and a voucher towards travel and expenses for the 2025 event. 

They're rewarding loyalty with _access_. 

They made their most loyal customers feel like **insiders**, not just repeat buyers.

Another foundational pillar of this event was the **aggressive integration of their digital ecosystem and first-party data capture**. 

To get access to the livestream details, exclusive merchandise drops, or a chance to attend the event live, consumers had to interact with the Taco Bell Rewards app. 

This is a brilliant growth hack.

While the audience felt like they were getting exclusive, VIP access to a secret club, Taco Bell was **actively migrating casual foot traffic into registered app users**.

Once a consumer is inside that app ecosystem, Taco Bell owns the relationship. 

They can bypass third-party ad networks, send hyper-targeted push notifications based on past ordering habits, and use gamified rewards to increase the lifetime value of that customer. 

The event served as the top-of-funnel hook for a highly sophisticated, data-driven retention engine.

Live Más LIVE is also aimed at the **celebrity-and-influencer culture**.

## Rachel Karten — Mystery is the best marketing

_From: `[email]` · 2026-05-28T15:34:35+00:00_

View this post on the web at https://www.milkkarten.net/p/mystery-is-the-best-marketing

Tomorrow the movie Backrooms [ https://substack.com/redirect/63316dda-fa36-4d3d-b88f-94cad8feac62?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] will play in theaters across the country. It’s directed by 20-year-old Kane Parsons [ https://substack.com/redirect/4d3ca45d-e310-4ebc-87af-6f8a31ac1e26?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] and is aiming [ https://substack.com/redirect/f010c043-ce60-4060-90d0-45fce0692971?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] for a $45M opening weekend. If I was being reductive, I would say that it’s a movie about a photo that was shared on 4chan. But really it’s a movie about everything around that photo. The myths, the questions, the short films, the Reddit threads.
What’s left unsaid leaves room for people to imagine. To superimpose themselves into the story. To build layers of lore. That way, by the time Backrooms reaches me—which it only did a few months ago—I have textbooks worth of knowledge to catch up on. Now I’m in their world too. Mystery is the best marketing.
“People want to be at the start of something. That’s our urge to be a part of the meta-narrative.”
I often get asked what it means to break through in culture. We used to look to views. Now, I’d argue its participation. When I study the most-watched videos on TikTok every month, I’m always surprised at how few actually broke through culturally. I know something is resonating today when the more interesting content is being made in comments sections and on personal accounts. Content about the content. The “red flats queen” video [ https://substack.com/redirect/eb69cb15-e799-4217-a6f8-33c039736329?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] from the Met Gala isn’t what made the moment break through. It was the speculation. Who is she? Where does she work? What’s going on?
In a conversation [ https://substack.com/redirect/4c228bcb-19af-45fd-8aa9-8e30c147c226?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] with Colin and Samir, creator Anthony Po talked about how the most crucial piece of his stunt accounts like Cheeseball Man [ https://substack.com/redirect/1e37bd20-8636-47b9-8745-37a482de8010?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] and John Chungus [ https://substack.com/redirect/88a298ef-b6ca-426c-932e-f084cf9c43a9?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] is to start it from scratch on a new page. He says, “People want to be at the start of something. That’s our urge to be a part of the meta-narrative.” That urge fuels participation. Anthony knew [ https://substack.com/redirect/534e3487-2034-4f81-a54b-c85f28bd4a31?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] John Chungus had momentum not when the views went up, but when fan edits [ https://substack.com/redirect/8b31d016-e90b-4b51-b400-d95faf907c11?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] rolled in.
That part about being “at the start of something” is important. There’s social currency to telling your friend about a funny video before their own algorithm does. It’s getting harder and harder to do. A few days ago I came across a brilliant Reel titled Anatomy of a Sheep [ https://substack.com/redirect/fa8dd676-4932-4727-98f1-d2b2be2c93aa?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ]. It had only 1,000 likes and the creator had less than 2,000 followers. I got the same feeling as when I was a teen and first heard a Coconut Records song or watched Blue Velvet. That euphoria of personal discovery that makes you want to fall down a wormhole into fandom. I thought I was at the start of it. The next day the video had 100K likes.
In a recent article [ https://substack.com/redirect/ef455ddb-c764-4937-aad9-0487665d83e8?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] by Amy Francombe  in Vogue Business, she writes, “As artificial intelligence accelerates replication, influencer culture reaches saturation, and global crisis seeps into the consumer consciousness, the industry’s reliance on scale as a proxy for value is losing traction.” She goes on to say, “This increasingly means brands trading spectacle for something harder to manufacture: meaning and connection, built through human relationships and stories that feel grounded in lived experience rather than engineered for scale.”
Amy talks about how luxury fashion brands are tapping into their own history as meta-narratives. Simon Porte Jacquemus naming [ https://substack.com/redirect/a2542e0a-9a3e-4232-ad34-c75ea88be59d?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] his grandmother as the brand’s first ambassador and Jonathan Anderson inviting [ https://substack.com/redirect/98f182b5-79d0-45be-beb7-8d2f0a312cff?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] Paulette Boncoure, an atelier artisan who started working at Dior in 1947, to the show. The post sharing the video of Paulette arriving has over 50K likes.
Denny’s case study
13 years ago, a video [ https://substack.com/redirect/ef759c23-eda3-429a-bf0a-eaafb2b6ae8f?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] of the band Live Without performing inside a Denny’s got 5.3M views on YouTube. A phrase from it—“What the fuck is up, Denny’s?!”—stuck. The conversation around it stayed active in the years since, with accounts celebrating its anniversary [ https://substack.com/redirect/cd4aac58-f3f5-4a0d-845d-4f41e1c8cfb3?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] and multiple Reddit threads [ https://substack.com/redirect/89fa1400-0902-45fe-823d-93c54af060ff?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ].
Last week, Denny’s finally collaborated [ https://substack.com/redirect/434d1513-1667-440a-9664-7c84520655b1?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] with the the band. The video has 3M views across platforms. A wink at the existing fandom, an invitation for a new one.
I had never seen the original video. But the web of super fans who were excited about the collab reverberated across the internet and right into my feed. I went down that same deep dive I did for Backrooms. Now I’m in their world too.
Below I spoke to the Sam Ellis [ https://substack.com/redirect/70ee1162-fedb-4aac-a920-bd019a3562db?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ], Head of Social at Denny’s, about the decision to finally lean in and why he trusted the audience would get it.
Rachel Karten: Can you take me into the early stages of the idea? Why was now the right time for Denny’s to reference this viral video?
Sam Ellis: I joined Denny’s just over a year ago and my first question was: “Why haven’t we reengaged the WTF moment?”
Doing what you do, you probably remember Denny’s was one of the first brands to really embrace social media in a distinctive way (our Tumblr era, as it were) and, over the past year or so, we’ve been intentionally reconnecting with that DNA and leaning back into a more social-first approach to marketing.
That approach is spearheaded by one simple idea: people want entertainment, not ads. And what’s more entertaining than “What the F#$@ is up, Denny’s?” So, once we solidified that strategy, we picked up the phone, called the band, and the rest is history.
Rachel: Were you at all worried about people recognizing the reference? I like how the teaser [ https://substack.com/redirect/a099a6cb-84ac-4b2d-886e-2fc6cc018fdc?j=eyJ1IjoiOGZ6aG43In0.MEdLiOcZRUc_N3oL6SgEUFCyFYN9tX8izo2S8jR1GNw ] served as a reminder.

Last May, after an insane season in both my personal and professional life, I decided to do something I’d never done before…
​
I took a sabbatical.

​
Normally, I love working. So taking time off felt… deeply uncomfortable. Like walking into a restaurant in ripped jeans and a tank top when it’s clearly a white-table-cloth situation.
​
For the last 5 years, my business has centered on brand partnerships and selling low-cost digital products ($99-$475), like Offer Breakthrough ( https://8419577a.click.convertkit-mail4.com/8ku408e4qmtoh262749ukhkomw72ptnn5d98p4o7dxxwknvdd95vekezoew9w0z8rq47ge49vqeg5lng277evq9g8ow382q8o0l02768kp527rm59r5vrkrnvqkaz04p4/wnhe45ewu6uqpqzrelhl/aHR0cHM6Ly9kZmwwLnVzL3MvOTAxMjBlNWM_ZW09bWFya3J1YmkyMDA2JTQwZ21haWwuY29t ).
​
But as 99.9% of digital product creators find out, there’s nothing passive about the income linked to them.
​
One-time purchases mean starting every month at zero. So you’re constantly in marketing mode, trying to find new customers.
​
Every. Single. Month.
​
The truth is, I was utterly and completely burned out. I knew I couldn’t keep going as-is.
​
The problem was I didn’t know what the next move looked like.
​
Every time I sat down, my brain spiralled into all the possible moves I could make. But I couldn’t see a clear path forward.
​
​I didn’t want to burn my business to the ground. There were still parts of it I really loved.​

## @benradack
Here's how I organize each ad set when testing 100 ads at once.

Start by identifying some kind of similarity between your creatives.

In this account, some ads targeted men, some targeted women, and some targeted both genders but focused on a specific problem.

I organized them into three batches.

→ Problem/solution → Men → Women
Why organize them this way instead of random groupings?
Because I'm still trying to learn something.

If the men ad set crushes and the women ad set struggles, I now know men are probably the stronger customer profile for this product. If the problem/solution ad set outperforms both gender focused ones, the audience cares more about the problem than who they are.

Even when you're batch testing fast for winners, you can still walk away with insights if you organize the ad sets with a purpose.

Try not to just randomly split 100 ads into 3 ad sets. Group them in a way that teaches you something while Meta does its work.

## @benradack
This is how I structure my creative tests when I actually want to learn something.

A real test isolates one variable. Otherwise you're just hoping for a winner.

My process:

→ Pick one thing to test (angle, hook, format, creator, LP)
→ Keep everything else the same
→ Launch in its own ad set with a set budget
→ Run for 4-7 days before making any decision
→ Judge on link CTR and ATC rate first, then CPA and ROAS once you have enough purchases to validate

The one variable rule is the whole game.

If you change the hook AND the thumbnail AND the copy AND the landing page and the ad wins, what did you actually learn? Nothing. You can't repeat it because you don't know what drove the result.

Example.

Testing angles for a supplement brand. Same format (static), same LP, same offer. The only thing that changes between ads is the message.

→ Ad 1: "Tastes better than your greens powder"
→ Ad 2: "Finally a vitamin you'll actually remember to take"
→ Ad 3: "Recommended by 500+ doctors"

Three different reasons to buy. Same everything else.

When one wins I know the angle resonated. Then I can take that winning angle and test it across different formats, hooks, and creators next.

This is how you build learnings over time instead of starting from scratch every week.

Test one thing. Learn. Build on it. Repeat.

Most native advertisers are optimising for the wrong metric.

CTR tells you whether the headline worked.
It tells you nothing about whether the advertorial worked.

I've seen campaigns with a 0.8% CTR outperform campaigns with a 1.4% CTR on CPA.

If people are reading 4 minutes and not converting, the CTA is broken.

CTR is the start of the diagnosis. Not the answer.

11 emails before he makes the first sale offer. Eleven. Every expensive lesson I’ve eaten in the last 10 years (in no particular order):

> First hire should be senior & NOT cheap. The cheap one always costs more in cleanup, every single time.

> Partnerships done on a handshake end badly. Doesn't matter how close you are to them.

> Tax bill on profit hits before the cash from inventory does. You can owe more than you have in the bank and not realize it until april = fucked

> Don’t rent your reputation, it costs more than letting them borrow money from you. Paid for this one in 2025, and I'll be paying for it through 2026 and 2027 and 2028.

> Profit share sounds like a dream until you actually run the numbers and how long it will take to get it into the whole “sharing” part.

> You can't out-earn a bad cofounder

> The win that gets you on stage isn't the win that pays the bills. Learned this one over and over, and I'll probably learn it again. Stages are needed to share what is being worked on backstage.

> 80% of your stress comes from 20% of your team or clients. Cut the 20% as fast as you can afford to

> The right office costs you less than the wrong one

> Product is always the most important thing. Marketing accelerates whatever quality and loyalty are already there. Bad product can't be saved by good marketing. EVER

> Reasons, Seasons, and Lifetimes. The faster you categorize people and projects into those three buckets

The Meta Performance Marketing Summit gave some insight into where the platform is going.

For those who didn’t make it, these were my two main takeaways:

(1) Media buying is having a resurgence, although it looks much different.

6-7 years ago you could create a lot of value with media buying tactics.

We then went through a phase where Meta forced simplicity and consolidation, and most of the value creation fell to content creation.

Moving forward, Meta seems invested in developing more tools for advertisers to align their incentives with Meta.

Whether it’s CASC, ROAS optimization, bid multipliers, etc, Meta has more ways than ever to configure your account. 

And a key aspect of media buying will be testing into and aligning the ad account with business objectives. 

(2) Enriching the product catalog is the future of GenAI creative on Meta.

This was probably the consensus “next step” from the summit, and is what I’m most excited about exploring with my team. 

Clean, clear data around your catalog is the bedrock for the future of Meta ads, and associating additional images and videos give meta the flexibility to fill all their inventory w quality, accurate ads

## @cjslattery
I’m getting some pushback from software guys, telling me I am undervaluing the full feature set of pieces of software.

Let me say that the full feature set used to its maximum potential is a useless metric. 

If 70% of your customers use 10% of your software’s capabilities, an AI replacement only needs to replace that bottom 10%, likely the most simple 10%, for it to cut your revenue by 70%. 

Almost nobody uses your product fully. And the more complex the product the smaller the percentage of users who take full advantage. 

I don’t need to replace everything triplewhale does to take a massive bite out of it. I just need to replace the 5 things that 50% of the user base uses it for.

Now this is something SaaS can work to prevent by more aggressively  getting customers to use more of the tool. 

But the fact remains, the actual value derived from average users is far below the theoretical maximum.
